headline_marked: [[Meta creates new non-voting stock class]] for Zuckerberg to pay tax, keep control
headline: Meta creates new non-voting stock class for Zuckerberg to pay tax, keep control
summary: Meta's new Class C non-voting stock allows founder Mark Zuckerberg to sell up to 10% of his economic stake to cover California's proposed $11 billion 'billionaire tax' without impacting his majority voting control.
details: Meta's board has approved a new class of non-voting Class C common stock, effective January. These shares grant ownership but no voting power in company decisions.

The New York Times reported that this new stock class is a strategic move for Mark Zuckerberg to pay California's proposed "billionaire tax" if it passes, without relinquishing his approximately 60% voting control.

Proposition 40, drafted by Berkeley tax law professors, proposes a one-time 5% wealth tax on California's resident billionaires. Backers estimate it could generate up to $100 billion over five years for healthcare, food assistance, and education.

According to the Times, Zuckerberg reportedly pressured Meta's board in September to devise a plan to shield him from the tax, even suggesting he would list his Palo Alto property for sale if no agreement was reached.
An SEC filing by Meta confirms that discussions regarding Proposition 40 influenced the creation of the new stock class, with Zuckerberg engaging board members on the topic as early as July.

The plan involves a one-time stock dividend: existing shareholders will receive one Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they own. This effectively acts as a two-for-one stock split that Meta states will not alter any shareholder's voting power.

This dividend will allow Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of his Class C common stock, representing 10% of his total economic stake, to cover his potential $11 billion tax liability under Proposition 40 without affecting his majority voting control.

Meta also stated that a motivation for this stock creation is to ensure Zuckerberg continues to lead the company from California, citing the importance of his close coordination with management and proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.

While other Silicon Valley leaders, like Google co-founder Sergey Brin, have actively campaigned against Prop 40, Meta's strategy suggests that major companies and their leaders are finding creative ways to address the tax should it be enacted.

topic: palmer luckey warhound military dog startup
headline_marked: [[Palmer Luckey's Warhound raises $200M]] for genetically enhanced military dogs
headline: Palmer Luckey's Warhound raises $200M for genetically enhanced military dogs
summary: The startup, co-founded by Anduril's Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences' Ben Lamm, aims to clone elite working dogs and equip them with advanced gear for military and law enforcement use.
details: Warhound, a new startup co-founded by Anduril's Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences' Ben Lamm, has launched with $200 million in funding. Its mission is to create genetically enhanced dogs for the US military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders, aiming to reduce dependency on European breeders.

The company is already gene-editing its first batch of dogs, collecting blood samples from "top-performing" military, police, and first responder canines to clone them. Breeds will primarily be Belgian Malinois, with some Labs and Shepherds, and the first puppies are anticipated by early 2027.

Initial gene-editing efforts will focus on eliminating common health conditions like hip dysplasia. Future plans include incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to "enhance" the military dogs' sense of smell, drawing on Colossal Biosciences' expertise.

Warhound will also equip its canines with "Anduril's advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness." While this sounds like cyborgs, the current plan involves tools like "advanced body armor" rather than embedded computers, according to Lamm.

Neither Luckey nor Lamm will be involved in Warhound's daily operations, though Lamm is on the board. David Spirk, formerly of the Department of Defense and Palantir, serves as CEO. Investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest, with Colossal Biosciences holding an ownership stake.
The project has been in development for over a year before coming out of stealth. Lamm described the concept as "like the Captain America dog program with the Ironman tech program on top of it."
The company plans to operate under the guidance of the American Humane Society.
